name: Micah Baptiste

biography.name: Micah Baptiste

background.family: Lives with his parents and older sister, with grandparents nearby; the family shares responsibilities and encourages interests beyond their small auto-parts business.
background.finances: Steady middle income with seasonal business pressures but no recent disruption to essentials.
background.cultureLanguages: Black American and Trinidadian family connections; English at home and conversational Spanish learned through school, neighbors, and customers.
background.school: Public high school with mock trial, robotics, choir, and ordinary laboratory science.
background.accessOpportunities: El Paso Community College events, UTEP outreach, libraries, and desert education programs are nearby; business shifts limit some weekends.

timeline.story: Micah liked making up trials in which stuffed animals argued about missing snacks. He was equally happy quietly arranging his sister's old costume jewelry into patterns, a habit adults rarely saw outside home.

He helped count inexpensive parts at the family shop and enjoyed asking what each item did. He disliked greasy equipment and learned that understanding a catalog did not require wanting to work on an engine.

A choir director noticed his sense of rhythm, and he liked the group sound. He also read mystery stories alone, often guessing an ending confidently and then defending the wrong guess long after new clues appeared.

He tried robotics with a friend and enjoyed building but lost patience with code. A teacher gave him a short public explanation to deliver; he sounded confident despite relying heavily on a teammate's understanding of the software.

Mock trial gave him enjoyable scripts and arguments. He began noticing that listening carefully could be more useful than speaking first. At the shop he learned to ask customers clarifying questions instead of guessing what they needed.

Micah left robotics for a season, then returned for a design challenge with more hands-on assembly. He made simple jewelry from discarded safe materials at home and showed it to friends only after they asked about a bracelet.

He balances mock trial, occasional choir projects, and shop shifts. A desert field outing has made him curious about outdoor science, though he has little camping experience. He is increasingly willing to say that an appealing possibility is something he has not actually tested.
